title: Cells
summary:
A cell is **a complete, independently runnable and deployable copy of the service**: app servers, data store, cache, queues, everything. **Cells never talk to each other.** A customer (or tenant, or key range) is assigned to exactly one cell, and a thin **router** in front maps the customer to it.

Picture **watertight compartments in a ship**: a breach floods one section, not the vessel.

- **Blast radius is 1/N.** A bad deploy, a poison request, a runaway query or a failed database affects only that cell's customers.
- **Cells are the unit of capacity.** Instead of scaling one giant system into untested territory, you cap each cell at a size you've load-tested and add more cells.
- **Cells are the unit of deployment.** Roll a change out cell by cell, small and internal cells first, and stop at the first sign of trouble.

The rules that keep it honest: no cross-cell calls and no shared state (a shared database makes the "cells" one failure domain again), a routing table that is simple and rarely changes, and the router and its mapping treated as the most critical shared piece.

Costs: more total capacity reserved, global features (cross-customer queries, global uniqueness) are hard, uneven cells need rebalancing, and moving a customer between cells is a migration ([rebalance](#/sd/f/rebalance)).

Related: [compartments](#/sd/f/compartment) are logical groupings that may or may not share hardware; [tenant isolation](#/sd/f/tenant-isolation) is the multi-tenant strategy; routing resembles [sharding](#/sd/f/sharding) but each shard is a full stack.

drills.q: A service runs in 20 identical cells with customers spread evenly. One cell goes down because of a bad deploy. What percentage of customers are affected?
drills.explain: One cell out of twenty carries 1/20 = 5% of customers. That bounded blast radius is the reason to build cells.

drills.q: Which of these break cell isolation? Select all that apply.
options: A database shared by every cell
Cell A calling cell B's API on each request
A router that maps customer id to a cell
Each cell having its own cache and database
drills.explain: Shared state and synchronous cross-cell calls turn all cells into one failure domain. The router is a necessary, deliberately simple shared component, and per-cell stores are the whole point.

drills.q: Why cap each cell at a tested size and add more cells, instead of growing one big cell?
options: Behavior at a size you've tested is predictable, and a failure's blast radius stays bounded
Small cells are cheaper per request
It removes the need for a router
drills.explain: A bigger single system hits untested limits (connection counts, lock contention, shard sizes) and takes more customers down when it fails. Cells trade some efficiency for predictability.

drills.q: Put a safe cell-by-cell rollout in order.
items: Deploy the change to a small internal or canary cell
Watch error rate and latency in that cell
Deploy to the next small group of cells
Continue in progressively larger waves while metrics stay healthy
Halt and roll back that cell if a regression appears
drills.explain: Cells make rollouts naturally incremental, so the first sign of trouble only touches a few customers. Rollback is local, too.

drills.q: A cell design places a single, shared 'user profile' database behind all cells for convenience. What is the main consequence?
options: A failure or overload of that database now affects all cells, so the blast radius is back to 100%
Cells can no longer be deployed independently of each other's code
Nothing: reads from a shared database are always safe
drills.explain: Isolation only holds to the extent that nothing is shared. Either put the data inside each cell (copy or partition it) or treat the shared dependency as the new top-level risk.

drills.q: Define a cell, and give two benefits and two costs.
drills.answer: A cell is a full, independently deployable copy of the service stack that serves a subset of customers and never talks to other cells. Benefits: bounded blast radius (1/N) and a tested unit of capacity and deployment. Costs: duplicated capacity and overhead, hard cross-cell/global features, a critical router, and migrations when moving customers between cells.
